title: I published my 2nd dataset! I turned SEC filings into 134 million queryable records.
author: NextgenAITrading
selftext:
My first dataset was House and Senate stock disclosures. For my second, I cleaned and normalized public SEC ownership data into a database with **10,054,299 insider transaction records** and **124,012,468 institutional holding records**.

The insider history goes back to 2006; the institutional holdings go back to 2013. I published the files as Parquet on Hugging Face and open-sourced the extraction pipeline on GitHub.

I wanted something I could download and query locally without setting up a scraper first. This downloads the published snapshot and builds a SQLite database:

    npx sec-ownership-disclosures download --sqlite

You can also download just one table and year if you don't need the whole thing:

    npx sec-ownership-disclosures download --table insider_transactions --year 2024 --sqlite

The interesting coding work was getting the records to mean what they appeared to mean:

* **Dates:** a transaction date and the date its filing became public are different. Each row has `availableAt` so historical queries can use the public filing clock.
* **Identifiers:** company names and ticker strings are messy. I kept the raw values and added `resolvedTicker` for price joins.
* **Amendments:** a correction stays a separate version instead of overwriting the original filing.
* **Verification:** downloads check SHA-256 hashes, and the audit re-parses the archived source files instead of trusting the ingestion counters.

The backfill also writes receipts so it can resume after an interruption.

The 13F records are quarterly holdings snapshots, so they don't tell you every trade a fund made. Insider records include sales, grants and option exercises too; the transaction codes let you separate those from open-market purchases.

* [GitHub repo, source and usage examples](https://github.com/austin-starks/sec-ownership-disclosures)
* [Dataset on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/austin-starks/sec-ownership-disclosures)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: keeping amendments as separate versions is the underrated part. an as-of query has to pick the version that was public on that day, otherwise a correction filed months later quietly leaks into anyone's backtest, and availableAt alone doesn't save you from that.

replies.author: NextgenAITrading
replies.body: Exactly! It's the little details that makes this data valuable for creating trading strategies... I take it that you've used this type of data yourself? What was your experience?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: not filings, no. I've only hit the same problem on price data, where a revision applied later makes an old backtest look cleaner than anything you could have traded that day. it's a big part of why I built Quantradin (quantradin.com), free and paper only, it runs a rule forward so it only ever sees what was public at the time.

replies.author: NextgenAITrading
replies.body: Super cool! is this a personal app or do you have a small team?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: small, a couple of us. most of the work has been the boring part, making sure the record can't quietly change after the fact.

replies.author: NextgenAITrading
replies.body: what do you mean? you mean like versioning your financial data and provenance?
